strengths: Compelling and practical motivation: addresses the significant compute and privacy barriers that prevent academic and clinical labs from pretraining high-resolution vision foundation models on in-domain data using desktop-class consumer GPUs.

Well-motivated technical adaptations: effectively solves numerical stability and efficiency bottlenecks when adapting off-the-grid hierarchical architectures (AutoFocusFormer) to MAE, including a softmax-temperature interpolation formulation and a Flash-style Triton cluster-attention kernel.
Insightful analysis of representation collapse: diagnoses token degeneration at deep, sparse stages via normalized effective rank analysis and provides an effective deep supervision remedy.

Impressive efficiency profile: demonstrates substantial FLOP and VRAM savings (e.g., ~7× FLOP reduction and ~2× VRAM reduction at 768×768 resolution) compared to standard ViT-MAE while retaining comparable segmentation performance on the evaluated task.
weaknesses: Extremely limited evaluation scope: the method is pretrained only on a private, in-house electron microscopy dataset (187k scans) and evaluated on a single small downstream dataset (FPW, 570 training images) for one specific task. There are no results on standard, established computer vision benchmarks (e.g., ImageNet-1k, ADE20K, COCO) or publicly available medical benchmarks (e.g., MoNuSeg, Cryo-ET, BraTS), making it difficult to assess generalizability.

Narrow baseline comparisons: the approach is only compared against a vanilla ViT-MAE baseline. Important hierarchical masked image modeling competitors (such as SimMIM, SwinMAE, or MixMAE) and relevant efficient vision backbones are omitted from the experimental comparison.

Incomplete reproducibility details: the link under the abstract ('Code available at') is left blank, and the datasets used for both pretraining and fine-tuning are private/in-house, preventing independent verification of the reported empirical gains.

Drafting inconsistencies and citation issues: the FLOP reduction claim varies between '6×' (Figure 1), '7×' (Abstract/Conclusion), and '13×' (Table 1 caption). In addition, several citations list the year 2026 (e.g., Tan et al., 2026; NVIDIA et al., 2026).

strengths: Practical and well-motivated problem: adapting Masked Autoencoders (MAE) to hierarchical, off-the-grid token-downsampling architectures so that high-resolution foundation models can be pretrained efficiently on consumer-grade desktop GPUs.

Solid technical and systems contributions to numerical stability: replacing the unstable inverse-power point interpolation with a temperature-softmax formulation, implementing a FlashAttention-style neighborhood cluster attention in Triton, and enabling stable fp16 mixed-precision pretraining.

Insightful analysis of representation collapse: the authors identify and visualize the rank collapse in deeper encoder stages under aggressive token pruning and effectively mitigate it using deep supervision, backed by normalized effective rank metrics and PCA projections.

Principled masking strategy: the use of Perlin masking for high-resolution biological imagery is well-motivated and supported by radial power spectral density (PSD) analysis comparing masks to natural signal statistics.

Convincing efficiency gains: the model achieves substantial reductions in computational cost (~4.5x to 7x reduction in FLOPs, ~50% lower VRAM, and higher training throughput) while matching the segmentation performance of a dense ViT-MAE baseline.
weaknesses: Overly narrow empirical evaluation: the experiments are conducted exclusively on an in-house electron microscopy dataset and a single small downstream segmentation benchmark (FPW). The paper would be significantly stronger with evaluations on standard vision benchmarks (e.g., ImageNet pretraining, ADE20K / COCO) or widely recognized public medical imaging benchmarks (e.g., Synapse, MoNuSeg, Cityscapes).

Missing hierarchical MAE baselines: while the related work section discusses hierarchical pretraining methods like SimMIM, SwinMAE, and MixMAE, none of these methods are included in the empirical comparison; the only baseline compared is standard isotropic ViT-MAE.

Modest architectural novelty: the core architecture heavily relies on AutoFocusFormer (Chen et al., 2023), with the primary contributions lying in systems optimization (Triton Flash-attention kernel), training stabilization (deep supervision, softmax interpolation), and Perlin noise masking.

Inconsistencies and drafting artifacts: 'Code available at' in the abstract is left blank; citation errors exist (e.g., 'Ziwen et al.' instead of 'Chen et al.' due to misinterpreting the first author's given name and surname); and FLOP reduction claims vary across sections (e.g., up to 6x in Fig. 1, 7x in Abstract/Sec. 4.2, and 13x in Table 1 caption).

strengths: Clear practical motivation: Enabling efficient in-domain foundation model pretraining on consumer/desktop hardware under institutional and data governance constraints (e.g., HIPAA/IRB) is an important and realistic problem in biomedical imaging.

Sound systems and technical design: The paper identifies specific failure modes when adapting off-grid hierarchical models to MAE—notably numerical instability in inverse-distance interpolation under AMP and feature collapse at sparse deeper stages. The proposed solutions (softmax-temperature interpolation, Triton Flash-style cluster attention, and deep supervision) are well-motivated.
Insightful representation analysis: The use of normalized effective rank and PCA visualizations provides concrete technical justification for the inclusion of deep supervision.

Compelling computational efficiency: Compared to a ViT-MAE baseline at 768x768 resolution, AFFMAE reduces FLOPs by ~7x and peak VRAM by roughly half while retaining comparable downstream segmentation mIoU.
weaknesses: Very narrow experimental evaluation: The framework is evaluated exclusively on a single downstream task (semantic segmentation on the Foot Process Width dataset containing only 570 training images) using a single, non-public in-house pretraining dataset (187k EM scans). The absence of evaluations on standard vision benchmarks (e.g., ADE20K, Cityscapes, COCO) or diverse public medical imaging datasets leaves the generalizability of the approach unverified.

Missing comparisons with hierarchical MIM baselines: While Section 2 discusses existing hierarchical masked pretraining architectures (such as SimMIM, SwinMAE, and MixMAE), none of these methods are included in the empirical benchmark. The comparison is restricted solely to standard isotropic ViT-MAE.

Limited evaluation protocols: Masked autoencoding frameworks typically validate representation quality through multiple probe protocols, including linear probing, attentive probing, and fine-tuning across different downstream tasks. Only fine-tuning for semantic segmentation is presented here.

Reproducibility concerns: The pretraining dataset is proprietary/in-house, and the paper contains an incomplete code availability placeholder ('Code available at' with no link in the abstract), making verification and independent replication challenging.

strengths: Strong practical motivation: The paper tackles a well-defined bottleneck in biomedical imaging where institutional privacy constraints (HIPAA/IRB) and huge image resolutions prevent transferring data to cloud clusters, making efficient desktop-scale pre-training highly valuable.

Well-engineered system solutions: The inclusion of Triton-based Flash cluster attention, cached KNN table lookup for the point decoder, and numerically stable exponential distance weighting directly addresses real-world memory and throughput bottlenecks in off-the-grid architectures.

Insightful diagnosis of feature collapse: The paper identifies that aggressive irregular token downsampling during MIM leads to severe rank degradation and semantic loss at deeper stages, and convincingly demonstrates that deep supervision with intermediate reconstruction heads restores normalized effective rank across stages.

Solid empirical results: AFFMAE achieves competitive or superior downstream segmentation performance compared to dense ViT-MAE and multiple hierarchical MIM baselines (SimMIM, HiViT, GreenMIM, MixMAE), notably outperforming them on ultra-thin biological structures (filtration slits) while delivering significant pre-training and fine-tuning throughput speedups and VRAM reductions across multiple resolutions.
weaknesses: Incremental architectural novelty: The core backbone heavily relies on AutoFocusFormer (AFF) and standard MAE principles. While the systems improvements, deep supervision, and Perlin masking adapt AFF nicely to masked pre-training, the underlying vision model remains largely that of prior work.

Domain scope restricted to microscopy: The evaluation is concentrated on electron microscopy datasets (FPW, Lucchi++, Kasthuri++, ISBI 2012). While this aligns with the stated motivation, evaluating the framework on standard high-resolution natural image benchmarks (e.g., Cityscapes or COCO) would better demonstrate whether the method generalizes beyond EM imagery.
Incomplete text in submission: The abstract ends with an unfinished sentence ('Code available at '), omitting the repository reference or an explicit note on code release upon acceptance.

strengths: Practical and timely motivation: In-house pre-training on consumer/desktop hardware is vital for biomedical settings constrained by HIPAA/IRB data governance and high-resolution imaging demands where thin structures cannot be downsampled.

Well-engineered and sound technical adaptations: Effectively adapts off-the-grid adaptive downsampling (AutoFocusFormer) into an MAE pipeline by addressing key practical hurdles—stabilizing the point-based decoder via an exponential distance kernel for mixed-precision arithmetic, introducing Flash-style Triton cluster attention kernels, and accelerating query lookups with quantized KNN caching.

Principled masking and supervision design: The inclusion of deep supervision is rigorously motivated and verified by analyzing the normalized effective rank across layers to prevent representation collapse in sparse stages. Similarly, Perlin noise masking is well-grounded through radial power spectral density (PSD) analysis.

Strong empirical results and efficiency gains: Demonstrates significant wall-clock speedups (up to 5x during 1024px fine-tuning) and roughly 50% VRAM reductions compared to standard ViT-MAE, while substantially outperforming other hierarchical MIM baselines (SimMIM, MixMAE, GreenMIM, HiViT) on narrow anatomical targets such as filtration slits.
Comprehensive validation: In addition to the primary kidney EM dataset, the authors validate generalization on multiple public microscopy benchmarks (Lucchi++, Kasthuri++, ISBI EM Challenge).
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental: The core backbone relies directly on AutoFocusFormer (Ziwen et al., CVPR 2023). While adapting it to MAE and providing Triton implementations/numerical fixes are non-trivial engineering feats, the conceptual architecture remains closely derived from prior work.

Limited evaluation outside microscopy: Although the paper intentionally frames its scope around biomedical microscopy, evaluating on standard general vision benchmarks (e.g., ImageNet-1K pre-training and downstream dense prediction on ADE20K or COCO) would help establish whether off-grid MAE pretraining offers universal benefits for general computer vision.

Sensitivity and overhead analysis: The paper does not thoroughly analyze the sensitivity of the exponential distance parameter $p$ in virtual token construction, nor does it quantify the training overhead added by the auxiliary deep supervision heads.
Minor presentation issues: On page 1, the code link is left incomplete ("Code available at"), and reference [22] contains an anomalous future publication year (2026).

strengths: Practical motivation and domain relevance: High-resolution biomedical image pre-training on local workstation hardware is an important practical problem, particularly due to privacy/data governance constraints (e.g., HIPAA) and the quadratic cost of standard ViTs.

Well-motivated integration of off-grid dynamic downsampling with MAE: Adapting AutoFocusFormer (AFF) to masked autoencoding avoids the rigid lattice requirements of standard hierarchical transformers (like Swin), allowing the encoder to process only visible tokens without architectural discrepancies between pre-training and fine-tuning.

Sound engineering and algorithmic enhancements: The paper introduces several sensible technical solutions to adapt AFF to the MAE setting, including replacing the numerically unstable inverse-power kernel with a softmax-based exponential distance kernel, Triton-based Flash cluster attention, an O(1) quantized KNN cache table for the decoder, and deep supervision to prevent representation/rank collapse in sparse deep layers.

Frequency-based justification for masking: Grounding the Perlin masking strategy in power spectral density (PSD) analysis to match the 1/f decay of biological structures is insightful and well-substantiated.

Convincing efficiency and fine-grained segmentation gains: AFFMAE achieves 2x pre-training speedup and up to 5x fine-tuning speedup at 1024px over standard ViT-MAE while retaining or outperforming ViT-MAE on fine, narrow structures (such as podocyte filtration slits) where standard hierarchical grid-based models suffer.
weaknesses: Incremental architectural novelty: The core backbone mechanics (cluster attention, adaptive off-the-grid token merging) are directly adopted from AutoFocusFormer (CVPR 2023). While adapting it to MAE with deep supervision and Triton acceleration is practically valuable, the overarching architectural novelty is moderate.

Heavy reliance on a private/niche dataset for primary claims: The main downstream benchmark (Foot Process Width dataset with 187k pre-training images) is private and domain-specific. While evaluations on public EM datasets (Lucchi++, Kasthuri++, ISBI EM) are included, the results there show essentially parity with standard MAE rather than a decisive accuracy lead.

Hardware accessibility framing: The claim of enabling training on 'desktop hardware' is supported primarily by experiments on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 (a flagship 32 GB GPU). It would strengthen the accessibility narrative to demonstrate pre-training feasibility on more widely accessible 16 GB or 24 GB consumer GPUs (e.g., RTX 3080/4080/3090/4090).

Incomplete pre-training wall-clock comparisons: In Table 5, pre-training wall-clock comparisons are only provided against ViT-MAE and SimMIM because other baselines (GreenMIM, HiViT, MixMAE) were trained on different hardware (H100), limiting direct wall-clock benchmarking across all competing hierarchical MIM approaches.
